title: The Same Path, in a Window

questions.question: What actually differs between drawing a path in a terminal and drawing it in a window?
options: The shape of one cell, and the size of the surface, both of which are already arguments
Everything, since one prints characters and the other paints pixels
The coordinate system is upside down in only one of them
The window needs the path stored differently
questions.explanation: Fitting, centring and flipping are identical. When a second surface costs one new argument, the first version was written at the right altitude.

questions.question: Why is the aspect 2 for a terminal and 1 for a window?
options: A character cell is about twice as tall as it is wide, so a metre across costs twice as many columns as a metre up costs rows, while a pixel is square
Terminals have half the resolution
The window has a margin and the terminal does not
Characters are drawn at twice the scale
questions.explanation: Both numbers describe round. What round looks like depends on what the surface is made of, which is exactly the thing worth passing in rather than baking in.

questions.question: The mapping returns across and down rather than x and y. Why does the naming matter?
options: Down is the direction the number grows, which is the opposite of the robot's y, and calling it y invites the mistake the flip exists to prevent
It avoids a name collision with the Pose
Qt requires those names
It makes the struct smaller
questions.explanation: This family of functions has enough coordinate systems in it already without a name that means two different things.

questions.question: Sixty columns of terminal fit a path into fifty nine steps, but four hundred pixels fit into four hundred. Why?
options: A character grid is indexed by cell, so the span is between the first centre and the last, while a window is continuous
The window reserves a pixel for the border
Terminals count from one
It is a rounding convention with no reason behind it
questions.explanation: This is what an off by one looks like when it does not crash anything: a picture very slightly too big, for years. The tests pin both answers so the difference is visible rather than absorbed.

questions.question: Most of the tests in this lesson draw nothing at all. Why is that possible?
options: The arithmetic is separate from the drawing, so it can be checked without a window, a screen or an event loop
Because Qt cannot be tested
Because the drawing is too slow to test
The rendering tests were left for phase 10
questions.explanation: Of the forty or so lines in the widget, the only one doing any thinking calls the function you wrote. That ratio is what a good boundary between arithmetic and a user interface looks like.

questions.question: This lesson is marked optional. What does a learner without Qt lose?
options: Nothing that anything later depends on, since 00-07 already drew the path with the same arithmetic
The whole of phase 00's payoff
The graduated mapping, which later lessons need
The ability to draw at all until phase 10
questions.explanation: That is why the terminal version is the required one and this is the bonus. An installation should never stand between a beginner and their first payoff.
